description: Assigning one variable to another copies the whole object.
correct_belief: Assigning an object copies the reference; both names now refer to the same object.
analogy: Writing a friend's address on a second sticky note doesn't build a second house. Both notes lead to the same front door.
socratic: If b = a made a full copy, what would print after b.append(4) followed by print(a)?
Python shows a and b with the same id(). How could two separate copies share one identity?

description: Passing an object to a function gives the function its own private copy.
correct_belief: The function receives a reference to the same object, so mutations inside the function are visible to the caller.
analogy: Lending someone the key to your locker doesn't give them a new locker. Whatever they rearrange inside, you'll find rearranged.
socratic: If the function had a private copy, why does the caller's list change after the function calls lst.append(9)?
What would it cost in time and memory to copy a million-element list on every function call?

description: Array indices start at 1, so the last element of an n-element array is at index n.
correct_belief: Indices start at 0, so the last element is at index n-1.
analogy: Floor numbering in many countries starts at the ground floor (0). The first floor up is floor 1, and a 5-storey building's top floor is floor 4.
socratic: If the last element of [10, 20, 30] were at index 3, what is stored at index 0?
The address of a[i] is base + i*size. Which i gives the very first element's address?

description: Inserting at the front of an array is O(1), just like appending.
correct_belief: Inserting at the front shifts every existing element one slot right, so it is O(n).
analogy: Adding a person to the front of a cinema row means everyone already seated has to shuffle one seat over.
socratic: After inserting at index 0, where does the element that used to be at index 0 go? And the one after it?
Elements are contiguous. If nothing moved, where would the new element physically live?

description: Accessing the i-th element of an array takes O(i) time because the computer walks from the start.
correct_belief: Array access is O(1): the address is computed directly as base + i * element_size.
analogy: Finding seat 47 in a numbered row doesn't mean counting 47 seats. You walk straight to the number on the armrest.
socratic: If elements are contiguous and all the same size, can you compute where element i lives without visiting the others?
Why do linked lists need to walk from the head, but arrays don't?

description: O(2n) is a different (worse) complexity class than O(n), i.e. believing constants change the class.
correct_belief: Constant factors are dropped: O(2n) is the same class as O(n).
analogy: Whether a road trip takes 2 hours per 100 km or 1 hour per 100 km, doubling the distance doubles the time either way. The growth pattern is the same.
socratic: If n doubles, by what factor do 2n and n each grow?
If O(2n) were its own class, would O(n + n) be different from O(2n)?

description: Big-O gives the exact number of steps an algorithm takes.
correct_belief: Big-O describes how the cost grows as input grows (an upper bound on the growth rate), not an exact step count.
analogy: Saying a city's population is 'in the millions' tells you its scale, not the exact head count.
socratic: Two loops each doing n steps and one loop doing n steps are both O(n). Do they take the exact same number of steps?
Why would we ignore machine speed and constant overhead when comparing algorithms?

description: A loop that halves n each iteration runs O(n) times.
correct_belief: Halving n each step reaches 1 after about log2 n steps, so it is O(log n).
analogy: Guessing a number from 1 to 1,000,000 by always splitting the range in half takes about 20 guesses, not a million.
socratic: Starting at n = 1024 and halving each time, how many steps until n = 1?
If n doubles to 2048, how many extra steps does the halving loop need?

description: Recursion stops automatically without a base case.
correct_belief: Without a base case nothing stops the calls; the function recurses until the stack overflows (or crashes on a null/None value).
analogy: Two mirrors facing each other: nothing makes the reflections stop by themselves. Something has to break the chain.
socratic: If countdown(n) always calls countdown(n - 1), what call happens right after countdown(0)?
Which line in the function would ever return without calling itself again?

description: The recursive call doesn't need to move toward the base case; reaching it eventually is enough.
correct_belief: Each recursive call must make the problem strictly smaller so it is guaranteed to reach the base case.
analogy: Walking toward a door only gets you there if every step actually brings you closer. Stepping in place forever never arrives.
socratic: If f(n) calls f(n) again, how is the second call any closer to the base case?
With base case n == 0, what happens when f(n) calls f(n + 1) for n = 3?

description: All recursive calls share the same local variables.
correct_belief: Each call gets its own stack frame with its own copy of parameters and local variables.
analogy: Each person in a relay race carries their own water bottle. Drinking from yours doesn't empty the next runner's.
socratic: If every call shared one variable n, what would fact(3) see in n after fact(2) and fact(1) have run?
Why can factorial multiply n * fact(n - 1) correctly after the inner call returns?

description: The deepest recursive call returns its value straight to the original caller.
correct_belief: Each call returns to its immediate caller, whose frame resumes and may do more work before returning.
analogy: Passing a bucket down a line of people: each person hands it to the neighbour who handed them work, not straight to the end of the line.
socratic: In return n * fact(n - 1), who performs the multiplication after fact(n - 1) returns?
If the deepest call jumped straight back to the start, when would the pending multiplications run?

description: You can access the k-th node of a linked list in O(1), like an array.
correct_belief: Nodes are scattered in memory; reaching the k-th node requires following k next pointers, O(k).
analogy: A scavenger hunt: each clue tells you where the next one is. You can't jump to clue 7 without reading clues 1 to 6.
socratic: Given only the head reference, where in memory is the 5th node?
Since nodes aren't contiguous, what address formula could compute node k's location?

description: Deleting a node only requires removing that node; the previous node's pointer doesn't need updating.
correct_belief: To delete a node you must set the previous node's next to the deleted node's next.
analogy: Removing a link from a chain leaves two loose ends. You must clip the remaining links together or the chain falls apart.
socratic: After deleting node B in A -> B -> C, what does A.next still point to?
Walking from the head after the 'deletion', which node would you still visit?

description: A stack removes the oldest item first.
correct_belief: A stack is LIFO: pop removes the most recently pushed item.
analogy: A stack of plates: you take the plate from the top, the one you put down last.
socratic: After push(1), push(2), push(3), which plate is on top?
If pop returned the oldest item, how would 'undo' in an editor undo your most recent action?

description: Popping an empty stack is harmless and just returns nothing.
correct_belief: Popping an empty stack is an underflow error; code must check is_empty() first.
analogy: Reaching for a plate in an empty cupboard doesn't give you a 'nothing plate'. You come away empty-handed and dinner fails.
socratic: If pop() on an empty stack silently returned None, how would a bracket checker tell 'no match' from a valid value?
What should a parser do when it sees ')' and the stack is empty?

description: A queue removes the most recently added item.
correct_belief: A queue is FIFO: dequeue removes the item that has waited longest (the oldest).
analogy: A line at a coffee shop: the person who arrived first is served first, not the one who just walked in.
socratic: After enqueue(A), enqueue(B), enqueue(C), who has waited longest?
If a print queue removed the newest job first, what happens to a job sent at 9am on a busy day?

description: Dequeuing from a queue always requires shifting every element, so it is O(n).
correct_belief: With a circular buffer (moving front index) or a linked list, dequeue is O(1).
analogy: At a deli counter with ticket numbers, nobody moves when someone is served. The 'now serving' number just goes up by one.
socratic: What if instead of moving elements we just moved a 'front' index forward by one?
With a linked list keeping head and tail references, how many pointers change on dequeue?

description: A good hash function produces a unique value for every possible key, so there are no collisions.
correct_belief: With more possible keys than slots, collisions are unavoidable (pigeonhole principle); a good hash spreads keys evenly.
analogy: With 366 possible birthdays and a class of 400 students, at least two must share a birthday, however you assign them.
socratic: How many distinct strings exist versus how many slots are in a 16-slot table?
If 17 keys go into 16 slots, can every slot hold at most one key?

description: The same key can hash to different values at different times.
correct_belief: A hash function must be deterministic: the same key always produces the same hash.
analogy: A library's shelving rule must always send the same book to the same shelf, or nobody could ever find it again.
socratic: If put('cat') used bucket 3 but get('cat') computed bucket 7, what would get return?
What property must hash(key) have for lookups to work at all?

description: Collisions mean the table is full.
correct_belief: A collision just means two keys map to the same bucket; it can happen in a mostly empty table and is resolved by chaining or probing.
analogy: Two guests assigned the same hotel room number doesn't mean the hotel is full. The desk just needs a rule for where the second guest goes.
socratic: Can two keys collide in a 100-slot table that holds only 2 entries?
With chaining, what happens to the second key that lands in an occupied bucket?

description: Hash table lookups are always O(1), even in the worst case.
correct_belief: Average lookup is O(1), but if many keys collide into one bucket the worst case is O(n).
analogy: An express checkout is fast on average, but if everyone picks the same lane you still wait behind the whole crowd.
socratic: If every key hashed to bucket 0 with chaining, how long is that chain after n inserts?
What does a lookup have to do with that chain to find the last key?

description: A node's depth and height are the same thing.
correct_belief: Depth counts edges from the root down to the node; height counts edges on the longest path from the node down to a leaf.
analogy: Depth is how many floors you've gone down from the rooftop; height is how many floors are still below you.
socratic: The root has depth 0. Does it also have height 0 in a tree with three levels?
A leaf has height 0. Must every leaf have depth 0 too?

description: A node in a tree can have more than one parent.
correct_belief: Every node except the root has exactly one parent; allowing two parents makes it a graph, not a tree.
analogy: A company org chart: each employee reports to exactly one manager. Two managers would make it a matrix, not a tree.
socratic: If node D had parents B and C, how many different paths lead from the root to D?
Trees have exactly n - 1 edges for n nodes. What happens to that count if a node gets a second parent?

description: A binary tree with n nodes always has height about log2 n.
correct_belief: Height ranges from about log2 n for a balanced tree up to n - 1 for a degenerate chain.
analogy: A family tree where everyone has exactly one child is still a binary tree. It's just a very tall, thin one.
socratic: What is the height of a binary tree where every node has only a right child?
Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order into a BST produces what shape?

description: In a binary tree each node must have exactly two children.
correct_belief: Each node has at most two children: zero, one or two.
analogy: 'Binary' means at most two doors out of each room, and some rooms are dead ends.
socratic: If every node had exactly two children, could the tree ever end?
What do we call a node with zero children?

description: In-order traversal of a BST gives an unsorted sequence.
correct_belief: In-order (left, node, right) visits BST keys in ascending sorted order.
analogy: Reading a well-shelved library left to right: every shelf on the left holds earlier call numbers, so a left-to-right walk reads them in order.
socratic: In-order visits the entire left subtree before the node. In a BST, how do those keys compare to the node?
Try in-order on the BST 8(3, 10). Is the output sorted?

description: Pre-order traversal visits the children before the node itself.
correct_belief: Pre-order visits the node first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree; post-order visits the node last.
analogy: 'Pre' as in preface: the chapter title (node) comes before its sections (children).
socratic: In pre-order on A(B, C), what is printed first?
Which traversal would you use to delete a tree safely, children before parent?

description: Only the direct children must be ordered, not the whole subtree.
correct_belief: Every key in the entire left subtree must be smaller than the node, and every key in the entire right subtree larger.
analogy: A sorted bookshelf is not just 'each book is in order with its neighbours'. Every book on the left half must come before every book on the right half.
socratic: In 10(5(_, 12), 15), each parent-child pair looks ordered. Where would a search for 12 go at the root?
If search can't find 12, is the tree a valid BST?

description: A binary search tree must be balanced.
correct_belief: The BST property only constrains ordering; a BST can be completely unbalanced (even a chain).
analogy: A dictionary sorted alphabetically is still sorted even if every word happens to start with 'z'. Order and shape are separate questions.
socratic: Insert 1, 2, 3, 4 into an empty BST. Is every node's ordering rule satisfied?
Why do balanced variants like AVL trees exist if every BST were already balanced?

description: Searching a BST requires checking every node, like searching a list.
correct_belief: At each node you compare and go one way only, so search takes O(h) time.
analogy: Finding a word in a dictionary: you open the middle and discard half each time instead of reading every page.
socratic: Searching for 3 at root 8, why would you ever look in the right subtree?
How many nodes does a search visit in a balanced BST of 1,023 nodes?

description: New keys are inserted at the root (or swapped into the middle of the tree).
correct_belief: Insertion searches for the key and attaches it as a new leaf where the search fell off the tree.
analogy: A new book goes into the exact gap where it belongs on the shelf. You don't rebuild the shelf around it.
socratic: If 6 were placed at the root of 8(3, 10), where would 8 go, and is the tree still a BST?
Where does a search for 6 in 8(3, 10) end up?

description: A node with two children can be deleted by replacing it with either of its children.
correct_belief: Replace it with its in-order successor (or predecessor) to keep the BST property, then delete that node.
analogy: When a team captain leaves, you promote the person whose rank is closest, not just whoever stood nearest.
socratic: Delete 8 from 8(3(1, 6), 10). If 3 moves up, where do 6 and 10 go?
Which key in the tree is the smallest one bigger than 8?

description: The in-order successor of a node is always its right child.
correct_belief: The in-order successor is the leftmost (smallest) node in the right subtree.
analogy: The next name after yours in a sorted class list isn't necessarily the person to your right. It's the first name of everyone after you.
socratic: In 8(_, 12(10, 14)), which is bigger than 8 but smallest: 12 or 10?
From the right child, which direction do you walk to find the minimum?

description: A heap is fully sorted.
correct_belief: A heap only guarantees each parent is ordered relative to its children; siblings and levels are not sorted.
analogy: In a company every manager earns more than their direct reports, but that doesn't sort all employees by salary.
socratic: Is [1, 5, 2, 6, 7, 3] a valid min-heap? Is it sorted?
If a heap were sorted, why would extract-min need sift-down?

description: Inserting into a heap is O(1) because you just append to the end of the array.
correct_belief: After appending, the new element sifts up to restore the heap property, which is O(log n).
analogy: A new employee may join at the bottom of the chart but gets promoted up past every manager they outrank.
socratic: Append 0 to min-heap [1, 3, 2]. Is the heap property still true?
How many swaps can sift-up need in a heap of height h?

description: A priority queue serves items in the order they arrived (FIFO).
correct_belief: A priority queue always removes the highest-priority (e.g. smallest key) item, regardless of arrival order.
analogy: An emergency room treats the most urgent patient first, not whoever arrived earliest.
socratic: Insert priorities 5, 1, 3. Which comes out first from a min-priority queue?
If arrival order decided everything, what would the priorities be for?

description: Implementing a priority queue with a sorted array makes every operation O(1).
correct_belief: A sorted array gives O(1) remove-min but O(n) insert because elements must shift; a heap gives O(log n) for both.
analogy: A perfectly alphabetised filing cabinet is quick to read from the front, but every new folder forces you to shift the rest.
socratic: To insert 4 into sorted [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], how many elements move?
Over n inserts and n removals, which is faster overall: sorted array or heap?

description: An adjacency matrix is always more space-efficient than an adjacency list.
correct_belief: A matrix always uses O(V^2) space; a list uses O(V+E), which is far smaller for sparse graphs.
analogy: A seating chart with a cell for every pair of 10,000 people is huge even if each person knows only five others. A contact list is tiny.
socratic: A road network has 1,000,000 intersections and about 3 roads each. How many matrix cells versus list entries?
When would the matrix actually be the better choice?

description: In an undirected graph's adjacency list, each edge is stored once.
correct_belief: Each undirected edge {u, v} appears twice: v in u's list and u in v's list.
analogy: A friendship goes in both people's contact lists, not just one of them.
socratic: If edge A-B is stored only in A's list, how would BFS starting from B find A?
Summing all list lengths in an undirected graph gives what multiple of E?

description: BFS finds the shortest path in any weighted graph.
correct_belief: BFS finds shortest paths by number of edges, which only equals shortest distance in unweighted (or equal-weight) graphs; weighted graphs need Dijkstra.
analogy: Fewest train changes isn't the same as shortest travel time if one leg takes five hours.
socratic: Path A-C costs 10 directly; A-B-C costs 1 + 1. Which does BFS reach first, and which is shorter?
What information about edges does BFS ignore?

description: BFS doesn't need to mark nodes as visited.
correct_belief: Without a visited set, BFS re-enqueues nodes on cycles and can loop forever or blow up exponentially.
analogy: Exploring a maze without chalk marks means walking the same corridors again and again.
socratic: In the cycle A-B-C-A, starting at A without marking, what gets enqueued after C?
How many times could a node be enqueued if it has many neighbours?

description: DFS explores all neighbours of a node before going deeper.
correct_belief: That's BFS. DFS follows one neighbour as deep as possible, then backtracks.
analogy: Exploring a cave system by following one tunnel to its end before trying the next, not peeking into every entrance first.
socratic: Using a stack, after visiting A and pushing B and C, which node is popped next?
What data structure would you need to visit all neighbours first?

description: DFS on a graph will terminate without a visited set.
correct_belief: On graphs with cycles, DFS without a visited set revisits nodes forever; it needs to track visited nodes.
analogy: Following hallways without remembering where you've been, you can circle the same loop forever.
socratic: DFS from A in A-B, B-A without marking: what does the recursion do?
Why doesn't DFS on a tree need a visited set, while DFS on a graph does?
